description: A liter of seawater holds about 35 grams of salt. That salt has been building up for billions of years. Here is where it comes from.

hero.hook: Rivers run fresh. Oceans run salty. The secret is time and evaporation.

blocks.text: Oceans cover more than **70%** of the planet. On average, a liter of seawater holds about **35 grams of salt**. That is no accident: it is the result of a very long process.
Salt does not fall ready-made from the sky. It travels down from the continents, then stays trapped in the ocean.
As rain falls through the air, it picks up a little carbon dioxide and turns slightly acidic. When it lands on rock, it eats away at it gently: this is **chemical weathering**.

blocks.caption: Salt pans: evaporation concentrates the salt dissolved in seawater

blocks.text: Rivers then carry off the dissolved minerals, above all **sodium** and **chlorine**, the two ingredients of table salt. They pour them into the sea.
Underwater volcanoes and hot springs on the ocean floor add salts too. But most of it still comes from the continents.

sections.title: Salt comes from the land first

blocks.text: Good question: if rivers bring in salt, why is the water of the Rhone or the Seine not salty? Because the salt there is very dilute, and because river water is constantly renewed.

In the ocean it works differently. Under the Sun, the water **evaporates** and goes back up into the sky. The salt **stays**. Year after year, century after century, it builds up. This is what we call the [[hydrological cycle and salt accumulation]].

Salt water is **denser** (“heavier” for the same volume) than fresh water. At the poles, when surface water freezes, part of the salt is pushed out into the liquid water around it. That water grows denser still and sinks toward the bottom.
This movement helps drive the great ocean currents. Those currents carry heat and nutrients around the globe. Salt is not just a matter of taste: it is part of the planet's climate engine.

sections.title: Salt also keeps the oceans moving

blocks.text: Salinity is not the same everywhere. Near the equator, strong evaporation can concentrate the salt. Near big rivers or melting sea ice, the water is fresher. The Dead Sea is an extreme case: very little water leaves, and a lot of salt stays behind.
Seawater is salty because rivers bring minerals down from the continents, and because evaporation leaves the salt behind in the ocean. That build-up has been going on for billions of years.
